# Studs Terkel, Pulitzer Prize-Winning Chronicler of American Voices, Dies at 96

(CNN) -- Studs Terkel, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author, radio host, and activist celebrated for giving voice to ordinary Americans, died Friday at his Chicago home. He was 96.

Terkel had grown increasingly frail since the publication last year of his memoir, *Touch and Go*, according to Gordon Mayer, vice president of the Community Media Workshop, an organization Terkel had long supported. "I'm still in touch, but I'm ready to go," he remarked during what would be his final public appearance with the workshop—a nonprofit dedicated to recognizing Chicago journalists who take risks in their reporting.

"My dad led a long, full, eventful—sometimes tempestuous—satisfying life," his son Dan said in a statement. Workshop President Thom Clark added: "The last time I saw him, he was up, about, and mad as hell about the Cubs."

*iReport.com: Remembering the legacy of Studs Terkel*

Renowned for his intimate portraits of ordinary people—young and old, rich and poor—Terkel earned the Pulitzer Prize in 1985 for *The Good War*, his acclaimed oral history of World War II.

Though born in New York, Terkel was raised in Chicago, where his parents managed a small hotel. It was there, seated in the lobby, that he first absorbed the endless parade of arguments, disputes, and stories exchanged by the hotel's colorful cast of characters. "That hotel was far more of an education to me than the University of Chicago was," Terkel told CNN in 2000. This early immersion in the unfiltered voices of everyday life would ultimately shape his lifelong devotion to preserving oral histories. He was frequently found with tape recorder in hand, engaging the very people whose stories would form the foundation of his books.

Terkel became virtually synonymous with the art of oral history, prized for his unique ability to illuminate the experiences of the working class. "Oral history preceded the written word," he explained to CNN in 2000. "Oral history is having people tell their own stories and bringing it forth. That's what history's about: the oral history of the unknowns that make the wheel go 'round. And that's what I'm interested in."

In a 1995 conversation with CNN's Lou Waters, Terkel discussed his book *Coming of Age*, which chronicled the lives of individuals who had spent their entire lives as "scrappers." The book featured subjects between the ages of 70 and 95—a generation he affectionately called "the truth tellers."

"Who are the best historians? Who are the storytellers?" Terkel posed. "Who lived through the Great Depression of the '30s, World War II that changed the whole psyche and map of the world, a Cold War, Joe McCarthy, Vietnam, the '60s—so often dismissed today, though I believe it was an exhilarating and hopeful period—and, of course, the rise of computers and technology? Who are the best ones to tell the story? Those who've borne witness to it. And they're our storytellers."

Following the death of his wife in 1999, Terkel turned his attention to a book exploring mortality, eventually titled *Will the Circle Be Unbroken? Reflections on Death, Rebirth, and Hunger for a Faith*. "It's about life," he reflected in 2000 when discussing the project. "How can one talk about life without acknowledging that, at some point, it will end? It makes the value of life all the more precious."

Studs Terkel, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author, radio host, and lifelong activist who dedicated his career to capturing the voices of everyday Americans, died at his Chicago home on a Friday. He was 96 years old.

According to Gordon Mayer of the Community Media Workshop, Terkel had grown increasingly frail in the time following the publication of his memoir "Touch and Go," which was released the previous year. His declining health marked the final chapter of a life spent almost entirely devoted to listening to and preserving the stories of others.

Terkel's most celebrated literary achievement came in 1985, when he received the Pulitzer Prize for "The Good War," a sweeping oral history that gathered firsthand remembrances from those who lived through World War II. The book exemplified the approach that had defined his entire body of work: an unwavering commitment to portraying ordinary people from all walks of life, giving voice to individuals whose experiences might otherwise have gone unrecorded.

The roots of this passion traced back to Terkel's childhood in Chicago, where he grew up in his parents' small hotel. It was in the lobby of that modest establishment that a young Terkel first observed the raw, unfiltered drama of human life—watching guests argue, fight, and share their stories with one another. Studs Terkel, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author, radio host, and lifelong activist who spent more than half a century giving voice to the hopes, struggles, and daily lives of ordinary Americans, died Friday at his home in Chicago. He was 96.

His death was confirmed by his son, Dan Terkel, who said his father had grown increasingly frail over the past year, following the publication of his memoir "Touch and Go" in 2007. Though his health had declined, Terkel remained mentally sharp and engaged with the world almost until the end, family members said, still eager to talk politics, jazz, and the state of the nation with anyone who would sit with him.

Born Louis Terkel in New York City in 1912, he moved with his family to Chicago as a child, where his parents ran a rooming house and later a hotel. It was in the lobby of that hotel, listening to the endless parade of guests, workers, and travelers swap stories, argue, and confide in one another, that young Studs first developed his lifelong fascination with the unheralded voices of everyday life. He would later credit those childhood hours of eavesdropping and observation as the true origin of his life's work.

Terkel went on to study law at the University of Chicago, but he found himself drawn instead to radio, theater, and journalism. He adopted the nickname "Studs" — borrowed from the fictional Chicago tough guy Studs Lonigan — and began building a career as a broadcaster, eventually hosting a long-running radio program on WFMT in Chicago that became a platform for his interviews with writers, musicians, laborers, and everyday citizens alike.

It was through this work that Terkel pioneered a distinctive form of oral history, one built not around the powerful and famous but around the "unknowns," as he called them, whose labor and lives quietly shaped the nation. His books — including "Division Street: America," "Working," and "Hard Times: An Oral History of the Great Depression" — wove together the first-person testimonies of factory workers, waitresses, soldiers, and housewives into sweeping portraits of American life.

His crowning achievement came in 1985, when he won the Pulitzer Prize for "The Good War: An Oral History of World War II," a book that captured the conflict not through generals and statesmen but through the memories of soldiers, nurses, and civilians who lived through it. The book's title, drawn ironically from the era's own rhetoric, exemplified Terkel's gift for letting ordinary voices complicate and enrich the official record of history.

Throughout his life, Terkel remained a committed activist, supporting labor rights, civil rights, and progressive causes, and he never lost his conviction that history was made not by the powerful few but by the countless unnamed people who did the work of building and sustaining society. As he often put it, history belonged to "the unknowns that make the wheel go 'round" — a philosophy that guided every interview, every book, and every broadcast of his remarkable career.

Terkel is survived by his son, Dan, and by the vast body of recorded testimony he leaves behind — thousands of hours of conversation that stand as an enduring archive of the American experience in the twentieth century.

# CNN's Pulitzer Prize Recognition

CNN, one of the world's most prominent 24-hour news networks, has received recognition through Pulitzer Prizes—though it's important to note some nuances about how broadcast journalism relates to this historic award.

## Understanding the Pulitzer Prize Connection

The Pulitzer Prize, established in 1917 through the will of publisher Joseph Pulitzer, has traditionally been associated primarily with print journalism, literature, and musical composition. For many decades, the prize categories were exclusively reserved for newspapers and, later, online journalism tied to print publications.

However, in 2014, the Pulitzer board made a significant change by opening the National Reporting category to broadcast media that had a text component (such as accompanying digital articles). This shift allowed television networks like CNN to compete alongside traditional print outlets for the first time in certain categories.

## CNN's Journalistic Achievements

While CNN itself may not always be the primary awardee in the same way traditional newspapers are, the network has been recognized for exceptional journalism, particularly through:

- **International reporting** on crises, conflicts, and humanitarian issues
- **Investigative journalism** exposing corruption, injustice, or systemic failures
- **Breaking news coverage** of major global events
- **Documentary-style storytelling** that combines visual reporting with in-depth written analysis

CNN journalists and teams have earned recognition and prestigious honors for their coverage of significant world events, including conflicts, natural disasters, and social justice issues, often through partnerships with digital content that meets Pulitzer eligibility requirements.

## The Evolving Media Landscape

This intersection of broadcast journalism and the Pulitzer Prize reflects broader changes in how we consume and value news. As traditional boundaries between print, digital, and broadcast media continue to blur, organizations like CNN represent the evolving nature of journalism—one where storytelling format matters less than the rigor, accuracy, and impact of the reporting itself.

The recognition of broadcast networks in journalism's most prestigious awards signals an industry-wide acknowledgment that quality journalism can emerge from any medium, provided it maintains the standards of accuracy, ethics, and public service that the Pulitzer Prize has championed for over a century.

Terkel died Friday at his home in Chicago, according to his son, Dan Terkel. No cause of death was immediately given, though friends said his health had been declining in recent months.

His 1974 book "Working: People Talk About What They Do All Day and How They Feel About What They Do" became a landmark work, later adapted into a Broadway musical. It captured the dignity, frustration and humanity embedded in everyday labor.

Terkel was also a lifelong activist, unafraid to voice his progressive political views, and was blacklisted during the McCarthy era for his associations with leftist causes — an experience that only sharpened his commitment to amplifying marginalized voices.

Colleagues and admirers remembered him Friday as a singular figure in American letters.

Through interviews with soldiers, factory workers, and civilians, Terkel captured both the genuine heroism and the profound moral complexity of the conflict, refusing to let nostalgia obscure its brutal costs.
